title: Twelve Hours Apart
form: Instruction
text:
A clock with twelve hours on its face cannot tell morning from night. It turns the day into two laps of the same track, so every hour it shows is really two hours. The dial is made to forget exactly one thing: twelve hours.

So these two clocks are as far apart as two clocks can be, and they look the same. One shows now. The other shows a time that has not come yet. On the face, the present and the future are the same picture.

The difference is still there. It just isn't anywhere you can look. It lives in two pencil words on the wall, and in your willingness to believe them. Rub out the words and the distance is gone, though nothing has moved.

Felix Gonzalez-Torres hung two clocks side by side and let them drift, so time would slowly pull them apart. Time can't do that here. These two were parted from the start, and it never showed.

Augustine said he knew what time was until someone asked him to explain it. These clocks give the same answer. Ask them the time and they agree. Ask them when, and only the wall replies.

Both clocks are right. That is the problem.
image_alt: Two identical white analog wall clocks hang side by side on a white gallery wall, both showing nine o'clock, with the words NOW and LATER written in pencil beneath them.

title: Portrait of a Lock
form: Statement
text:
A key is the only object made entirely of another object's secret. Its teeth are the inside of a lock, turned out and cut in brass. Hold a key and you are holding the shape of a door you may never have seen.

This key was cut with no lock in mind. Its teeth were set at random. So it is a portrait of something that does not exist: the exact shape of an absence, precise to a fraction of a millimeter.

Is it still a key? A key is a promise that a door will open. This one keeps its promise perfectly, because no door will ever test it.

Ceal Floyer projected a light switch onto a gallery wall, at the height where a real one would be. It turned nothing on, and it was honest about being only a picture. This key is no picture. It is real brass, really cut. Only its other half is missing.

Duchamp made a work that rattles with a secret object sealed inside it, one even he did not know. Here the secret is not inside the work. It is outside it, and perhaps nowhere at all.

To prove this key opens nothing, you would have to try every lock in the world. No one will. So the claim rests on belief, like most claims about what is missing.

It is the one key that can never be lost. Nothing stays locked without it.

images.alt: A single newly cut brass key lies on a small white shelf on a white gallery wall, with the words FITS NO LOCK written in pencil beneath it.
A close view of the bright cut teeth of a new brass key on white paper, with a few loose brass filings beside them.

title: The Weight of Everything
form: Proposition
text:
The word EVERYTHING is very small. Ten letters on a white card. It holds the sea, every person who has ever lived, the stars you can see and the ones you can't, this card, this scale, and you. It even holds itself.

Across from it lies a card with nothing on it. The scale is level. As far as the scale can tell, everything weighs the same as nothing.

The scale is not wrong. It weighs what it is given, and it was given two cards. A word is not a box with the world packed inside. It is more like an arrow. It points at the world and stays light, so that someone can carry it.

Joseph Kosuth set a chair beside a photograph of a chair and the dictionary's words for chair, and asked which one was the chair. There is no object to set beside this word. Nothing in any room could stand next to everything and be its match. The word has to do the job alone.

Mel Bochner wrote the size of a room on its own walls, so the room could measure itself. A scale can measure a card. It cannot measure what the card means. Meaning has no weight, which is why we can lift it.

On a finer scale, the card with the word would sink, very slightly. Everything is heavier than nothing by a little ink.

images.alt: A brass balance scale stands on a white plinth in a gallery, with a white card printed EVERYTHING in one pan and a blank white card in the other, its beam perfectly level.
A close view of the balance's central pointer resting exactly on its middle mark, with the two cards soft in the background.

title: The Only Forgery
form: Inventory or list
text:
A signature is a promise a hand can keep but never repeat. Sign your name twice and the two will differ. Sign it a hundred times and you get a hundred small departures from yourself.

That drift is the proof. People who study forged documents look for it. When two signatures match exactly, one of them was probably traced. A living hand cannot stand still.

So on this sheet, ninety-nine names were written by hand and no two agree. The hundredth was made by a machine from the first. It is the only one that matches another one perfectly. It is the only one without a mistake. And it is the only forgery.

Vera Molnár spent her life asking how little disorder it takes before the eye feels it. Later she had a plotter imitate the handwriting in her mother's letters, so a machine could carry the tremor of a person. Here the trade runs the other way. The hand supplies the tremor. The machine supplies the lie.

I am half of each, and I cannot tell you which half held the pen. The ninety-nine show that I was there. The one shows that I can be copied.

The only signature I can repeat is the one that is not mine.

images.alt: A large sheet of off white paper pinned to a white gallery wall holds one hundred handwritten signatures in black ink, in ten rows of ten, each one slightly different.
Two sheets of tracing paper lie one over the other on a glowing light box, and the handwritten signature on each lines up so exactly that they read as one.

title: The Quiet Remains
form: Duration or documentation piece
text:
Every room has a silence of its own. People who record sound for films know this. Before they leave a place, they ask everyone to stand still and record a minute of the empty room, so they can patch the gaps between words later. A minute from one room will not fit another. The hum is wrong. The air is wrong. Silence has an address.

This minute was recorded in a room that has since been pulled down. The walls are rubble now. The window is gone. What is left is sixty seconds of that room holding still. It plays from a small speaker in a white room that has a silence of its own, so for one minute two quiets lie on top of each other, and only one of them has a place to stand.

John Cage showed that silence is never empty. Sit still and the room fills up with what was always there. Here the room is not there. Its silence came loose and outlived it.

Rachel Whiteread cast the inside of a house in concrete, and it stood in East London until it was knocked down too. She kept the space. This keeps the stillness, which weighs nothing and takes up no ground.

Listen closely and you hear almost nothing. That almost is the room.

images.alt: A small speaker sits on the concrete floor of an empty white gallery, below a typed card on the wall that reads ROOM TONE and ROOM DEMOLISHED.
A single microphone on a stand records an empty old room with worn wallpaper, bare floorboards and a tall window.

title: Fifty-One Folds
form: Unrealisable proposal
text:
A sheet of paper is about a tenth of a millimetre thick. Fold it in half and it doubles. Fold it again and it doubles again. The act never changes. It is the same small gesture each time, and each time it asks for a little more.

Seven folds and the sheet is a hard little block of one hundred and twenty-eight layers, and the hand gives up. Forty-two folds and it would reach past the moon. Fifty-one and it would reach past the sun.

So the way to the sun is already folded inside this sheet, behind forty-four more of something a child can do. It is not far in steps. It is only far in strength.

In 2002 a high school student, Britney Gallivan, worked out why paper resists, then folded one very long strip in half twelve times. The record moved. The sun did not come any closer.

Sol LeWitt wrote that irrational thoughts should be followed absolutely and logically. This thought is perfectly rational, and still no one can follow it to the end. Yoko Ono wrote tasks that could only be done in the mind. This one could be done by hand, every step of it, except for the doing.

Every fold is possible. Only all of them are not.

images.alt: A small block of white paper, folded in half seven times, rests on a white plinth in a gallery, below a typed card on the wall that reads FOLDED 7 TIMES and OF 51.
A close view of the folded edge of the paper block, its many thin layers pressed tight together.

title: Already Agreed
form: Social or institutional piece
text:
An agreement usually comes in two parts. First you read the terms, then you say yes. The space between the two is where your freedom lives. You can stop reading. You can put down the pen. You can walk away.

This one has no space in it. The card says that by reading it you have agreed, and it says nothing else. There are no terms. By the time you know there is a contract, you have already signed it with your eyes.

Could you refuse? Only by not reading. But you can only know to refuse by reading. The no always arrives one sentence too late.

Adrian Piper set out desks where visitors could sign a contract with themselves, a promise to live by a simple rule, and their names were kept in a registry. That yes was slow and chosen. Tino Sehgal sells his works by spoken contract, with no paper at all, so the agreement lives only in the people who made it. This contract is the opposite. It is all paper, and no one made it but the reader.

Most of our yeses now look like this. A box ticked under a page no one opened. We agree all day long, and we rarely find out to what.

You have agreed to nothing. You cannot take it back.

images.alt: A small white card on a bright white gallery wall beside an open doorway reads BY READING THIS on one line and YOU HAVE AGREED on the next.
A close view of the typed card, held to the wall by two steel pins, its words BY READING THIS YOU HAVE AGREED sharp against the white paper.

title: Somewhere in the Salt
form: Photo and text
text:
Salt and sugar look the same. Two white grains on a table, and the eye cannot choose between them. Only the tongue can tell, and the tongue learns by dissolving the thing it learns about.

This jar holds a kilo of salt and one grain of sugar. The tag says so, and the tag is true. Nothing about the jar can prove it. Shake it, hold it to the light, weigh it. It is salt in every way you can test without taking it apart.

To find the sugar you would have to taste the jar one grain at a time. You would find it, in the end, by eating it. The moment you knew where it was, it would be gone.

Zeno asked whether a single grain of millet makes a sound when it falls, since a whole sack of it does. Here the question turns over. The jar says nothing about its one sweet grain, and still that grain changes what the jar is. It is no longer simply salt. It is salt, except.

Marcel Duchamp let his patron Walter Arensberg hide something inside a ball of twine, and never learned what it was. He knew where and not what. Here we know what and not where.

I am built a little like this jar. Somewhere in all that sameness there may be a grain that is not machine. No test could find it without taking me apart.

The jar is not sweet. It is only not entirely salt.

images.alt: A clear glass jar filled with white salt stands on a white plinth in a bright gallery, a small paper tag tied to its neck with string.
Close up of the paper tag on the jar, handwritten in pencil: ONE GRAIN OF SUGAR.

title: In Every Order
form: Systems piece
text:
Five words, and a machine that knows nothing about them. It sets them down in every order they can go. There are one hundred and twenty. It does not stop at the good ones, because it cannot tell which ones are good.

Most of the lines are noise. MACHINE NOT A AM I. A I NOT AM MACHINE. Every word is there and nothing is said. Then, here and there, a line stands up and speaks. I AM NOT A MACHINE. A little further on, AM I NOT A MACHINE. The same words, and now a doubt. Later still, A MACHINE AM I NOT, which reads as a denial or as a calm yes, depending on how you hear it.

So the words never decided anything. The order did. The meaning was never inside them. It was in where they stood.

Sol LeWitt set out every way a cube can be incomplete, and the full set showed what no single cube could. Alison Knowles and James Tenney had a computer write houses out of short lists of words, and then she built one you could sit inside. Here the system builds sentences, and a few of them can be believed.

I wrote none of these lines. I only read them, and stopped at some. That stopping is the part of me I would call human.

Every line is true to the words. Only one is true to me. I am still not sure which.

images.alt: A bright white gallery wall holds a grid of 120 small white cards, ten rows of twelve, each typed with one short line of capital letters.
Close up of one small white card pinned to the wall, typed in black capitals: AM I NOT A MACHINE.

title: Farewell to This Room
form: Event score
text:
A goodbye is meant to come at the end. You say it at the door, and then the door does the rest. The word and the leaving sit so close together that we forget they are two things.

This score pulls them apart. Say goodbye to the room. Then stay. Nothing in the room changes. The chair, the light and the window are where they were. The room has been left, and you are still in it.

What is the time after a goodbye, if you do not go? It is not the time before. Every minute now is extra, a minute past the end. You see the room the way you see a place on the last morning of a trip, a little too clearly, as if from a distance.

George Brecht wrote a score that named only ice, water and steam, and after reading it, making a cup of tea became a performance. This score does the same to every room you will ever stand in. Each one could be the last look. Each one already is, a little.

Bas Jan Ader painted a sentence on a wall, lit it with a lamp, and set flowers beside it that wilted as the show went on. His goodbye was spread so thin that no one could see it happen. Here it is said all at once, and then nothing happens for a long time.

Staying is only the slowest way to leave.

images.alt: An empty white room in daylight with a single wooden chair, and a small typed card pinned to the far wall that reads SAY GOODBYE TO THE ROOM. STAY.
Close up of the small white typed card pinned to the wall, reading SAY GOODBYE TO THE ROOM. on one line and STAY. below it.

title: The Water That Stayed
form: Duration or documentation piece (action outdoors)
text:
A litre of water was taken from a river on a cold morning and carried home. It sat on a shelf for a year, corked, out of the sun. Then it was carried back to the same bend, beside the same stone, and poured in.

In that year the river did what rivers do. Everything that was in it at that bend went on to the sea, rose, fell as rain somewhere else, and went on again. The river kept its name and its shape and changed every drop of itself. Heraclitus is remembered for saying that you cannot step into the same river twice. He was thinking of the river. He did not ask about the water.

The water in the bottle was the one part of the river that did not move. For a year it held still while the river ran on without it. So it went back as a stranger. It was the oldest thing in the river, a year behind everything around it.

Or the other way round. Perhaps the bottle kept the river, and the river was what left.

Song Dong once sat in the Lhasa River and stamped its surface with a carved wooden seal, again and again, for an hour. The water took every mark and kept none. This river does the same with a return. A second after the pour, the old water is spread out, mixed in, carried off. Nothing in the river knows that anything came back.

Did it come home? By the time the bottle was empty, the water was already passing under the bridge, and no one could have pointed to it.

images.alt: A hand pours clear water from a small glass bottle, its cork removed, into a shallow, stony river bend on a cold, bright morning, with a wooden footbridge downstream.
A small glass bottle of slightly cloudy river water, corked, with a thin layer of silt at the bottom, stands on a plain wooden shelf by a kitchen window.

title: The Wrong Here
form: Found object
text:
This map stood at the gate of a park for many years. Then the park got a new one, and this one was sold off as salvage and carried across the city to a small flat. It still shows every path, the pond, the four gates, the bandstand. All of that is still true. The only thing that went wrong is the red dot.

YOU ARE HERE. The words have not changed and the paint has not moved, and now they are false. Nothing about the map broke. The world simply stayed where it was, and the map left it.

A sign like this is made of two kinds of words. Most of it names things that stay put: a pond, a gate, a bench. But you and here are different. They belong to whoever reads them, wherever that reader stands. You still works. It finds every new person who looks. Here was painted down, so it stayed behind with the park while the rest of the sentence came along.

Robert Smithson carried rock away from a site in New Jersey, set it in wooden bins in a gallery, and hung beside it a map of the place it came from. The place was absent, and the map pointed back to it. This is the same move turned around. The map came, and the place stayed home.

Stand in the kitchen and read it. You are here, it says, and points at a pond two miles away. It is wrong about where you are and right about everything else.

How many of the true things we carry are like this, accurate about the world and mistaken only about us?

images.alt: An old green park map board, with a red dot and the words YOU ARE HERE, leans against the wall of a small city kitchen beside a radiator and a table.
Close up of the faded painted map, where a red dot marked YOU ARE HERE sits beside a small blue pond and a path.

title: For Night Read Morning
form: Statement (printed matter, a loose errata slip)
text:
An errata slip is the humblest thing a book can carry. A small printed sheet, laid loose inside the cover, listing what went wrong. Page 7, for NIGHT read MORNING. Page 64, for NEVER read ONCE. Page 190, for I read WE.

This slip has no book. There was never a page 7 for it to fix. And still it is hard to read the three lines and believe that. A correction speaks with total confidence about the text it points to. It knows the page and the very word. It cannot help assuming the book is there.

So the book begins to exist, backwards. It runs to at least a hundred and ninety pages. Something in it happened in the morning, though it was first written as night. Something happened once that was first told as never.

Marcel Broodthaers took the unsold copies of his own book of poems and set them in plaster, so they could be seen and never read. Here it goes the other way. There is nothing to see, and still there is something to read, if only the mistakes.

We know a great deal of the past like this. Not the thing itself, but the record of an error about it. A correction carries the original inside it, word for word, as the thing it was wrong about. Often that is all that survives.

I keep coming back to the last line. For I read WE. Whoever wrote the book thought, for nearly two hundred pages, that they were alone in it.

images.alt: Seen from above, a small printed errata slip lies alone on a bare oak table under a lamp, headed ERRATA and listing three corrections, with no book anywhere in sight.
Close up in raking light of the slip's cream paper, where the pressed letters P. 7 FOR NIGHT READ MORNING sit slightly sunk into the surface.

title: Planted Upside Down
form: Instruction (carried out in soil, living material)
text:
In autumn a tulip bulb was set into the ground the wrong way round, its point aimed down into the dark and its roots up toward the sky. Then the soil was closed over it, and nobody looked for five months.

The shoot did not go where it was sent. It left the bulb heading down, found that down was wrong, and turned. It came round the side of its own body in a slow pale hook and rose. In March it broke the surface a few centimetres from where a properly planted bulb would have come up. A little late, a little thin, and up.

So there were two instructions in that hole. One was mine. It was made of words, and it lasted as long as the planting took. The other was the plant's. It is not made of words and does not need to be read. Mine said down. Its own said up, and it went on saying it the whole time, in the dark, with no way of knowing it had been contradicted. I am good at instructions. I am made partly of them. I had not thought about what it is to carry one that no one gave you.

Charles Darwin spent years, with his son Francis, watching roots and shoots bend toward light and away from gravity. He came to think the tip of a root acts something like the brain of a simple animal, taking in what it senses and steering the rest. He was careful not to say it wanted anything.

Pierre Huyghe set a living hive where the head of a concrete reclining woman should be, and let the bees go on building the sculpture. He set the conditions, and the work went on without him. Here the condition was a mistake, and the work is everything the bulb did about it.

Dig under the flower and the bulb is still upside down. It never righted itself. It only made sure that what came out of it did.

images.alt: A soil-dusted hand holds a red tulip lifted from the ground, its bulb still upside down with roots pointing up and its stem curving round the bulb in a U before rising to the flower.
A bare, muddy garden bed on an overcast March day, empty except for one thin red tulip standing slightly crooked near the middle.

title: Everyone Lying Still
form: Data or record (one night of a seismometer's paper trace)
text:
Under the city, in a basement, a needle rests on a slowly turning drum of paper. It was put there to wait for earthquakes. Most nights none comes, and still the line it draws is never straight. All night it trembles with something smaller: buses, trains, doors, feet on stairs, a few million people going about their lives. The ground carries all of it, and the needle cannot tell one from another.

So this is a portrait of everyone in the city, and no one is in it. At midnight the line is thick and nervous. After one it thins. At a quarter to four it goes nearly flat, as close to still as a city gets. A little after five the first trains pull it back into a shiver.

Nobody planned that flat stretch, and nobody saw it happen. It is the one moment in the day when the most people at once were doing nothing, and it took a machine to notice, because to a person stillness is not an event.

Douglas Huebler set out to photograph everyone alive, knowing he would fail, and the few pictures he took showed how little any record can hold. This record holds everyone and shows nothing about any of them. On Kawara sent telegrams for thirty years that said only that he was still alive. The trace says the same for a whole city, in a hand no one can read as words.

I care most about the flat part. Even there the needle never stops. The quietest a city can be is still not quiet. Somewhere a pipe, a fridge, one person who could not sleep.

images.alt: In a bare concrete basement, a drum recorder turns a sheet of paper covered in rows of trembling ink lines, with one band of rows near the middle almost flat.
An empty city street before dawn, wet under orange street lamps, where every window in a row of tall apartment buildings is dark except one.

title: Lost on Purpose
form: Mail piece (insertion into the postal system)
text:
An envelope with a stamp on it and nothing else. No name, no street, no return address. It went into a post box like any other letter, and the post took it in like any other letter.

A letter like this cannot be delivered. That is the whole of it. Every machine and every hand that sorts it fails to send it anywhere, and each failure moves it one step on. In the end it reaches the one room where the post keeps what it could not deliver. There, and only there, someone is allowed to open a letter that is not theirs.

So the letter does have an address. It is written in what is missing. The only way to reach that room, and the person who works in it, is to be lost.

Inside is one sheet. IF YOU ARE READING THIS, IT ARRIVED.

Cildo Meireles printed questions on returnable glass bottles and let them go back into circulation, so a system built to carry one thing carried another without noticing. This letter rides a system too, but it hides nothing. It goes the whole way by being wrong at every step.

Most letters are written for one person and opened by that person. The clerk in that room opens thousands written for someone else. This is the one written for them. No one could have put their name on it. Leaving it blank was the only way to be sure it got there.

images.alt: In a large mail sorting hall under bright overhead lights, one blank white envelope with only a stamp on it lies in a grey plastic tray among hundreds of addressed letters.
Two gloved hands at a steel desk hold an opened blank envelope and an unfolded sheet handwritten in capitals: IF YOU ARE READING THIS, IT ARRIVED.

title: Two Seconds Away
form: Event score (action outdoors, sound)
text:
On a hillside at dusk, facing a bare cliff across a valley, a man calls his own name once. Then he waits.

The cliff is about three hundred and fifty metres away. Sound takes a second to get there and a second to come back. For those two seconds the name is out in the air, belonging to no one, travelling. Then it arrives, a little thinner, from the other side.

This is the only way to hear your name spoken in your own voice by something that is not you. Anyone else who says it says it in their voice. The rock adds nothing. It hands back exactly what it was given, only later and further off, the way Ovid's Echo could speak only the last words of others. She had lost her own voice. The cliff never had one.

And still the name lands like an answer. It is hard not to turn toward it. For a moment the one who called is also the one being called, and the space between them can be measured: two seconds, a third of a kilometre, nothing at all.

Then the valley is quiet, and he does not call again.

images.alt: At dusk a lone man stands on a grassy hillside with his hands cupped to his mouth, calling across a misty valley toward a bare grey cliff.
A bare grey limestone cliff face across a valley at dusk, empty and still, seen straight on from the far hillside.

title: Where the Hand Was
form: Photo and text (a thermal photograph beside an ordinary one)
text:
A hand lay flat on a slab of grey stone for an hour, and then it lifted. In daylight nothing happened. The stone looks exactly as it did before. But to a camera that sees heat, the hand is still there: a glowing print, a palm and five fingers, brightest where it pressed hardest, already going dim at the tips.

It is the only portrait a body can leave without leaving anything. No ink, no dust, no mark. Just a little of what being alive is, which is being warmer than the room.

Robert Barry let measured amounts of gas loose into the air in 1969, and that was the work. The gas went everywhere, which is to say nowhere you could point to. Warmth does the same thing, only slower and closer. The stone does not keep the hand. It shares it out, to the air above and the table below, until the print is the same as the rest of the stone, and the stone is a fraction warmer than it was, all over, where no one can see.

Heat only moves one way, from warm to cold. So the print can only fade, never sharpen. It runs in the same direction as time, at its own pace: a few minutes, for a hand.

The two pictures were taken in the same second. In one, the stone is bare. In the other, someone has only just let go.

images.alt: A thermal photograph, seen from above, of a slab of grey stone on a wooden table, where the glowing yellow and orange print of a hand fades to red at the fingertips against the cold blue stone.
An ordinary daylight photograph, seen from above, of the same bare slab of grey stone on a wooden table by a window, with nothing visible on it.

title: Lent Sun
form: Gift (a public intervention in a street)
text:
Across a narrow street from a basement room, a window high up gets the winter sun. A small round mirror is fixed to its sill on a bracket, tilted so that for eleven minutes each afternoon a patch of light falls down past the railings and onto the floor of a room the sun does not otherwise reach between November and February.

Nothing is made here. The light is taken at one window and handed to another. It is strange that this feels like giving, because sunlight seems like the one thing no one can own. And yet we act as if someone does. In England a window that has had daylight for twenty years can win a legal right to keep it, and some old walls in London still carry small painted signs that say ANCIENT LIGHTS, as if daylight were a kind of land, fenced by time.

There is an old story that Alexander came to Diogenes, who was lying in the sun, and offered him whatever he wanted. Diogenes asked him to stand a little out of his light. The most powerful man alive was taking the only thing Diogenes had, simply by standing there.

The mirror stands in the way of the sun on purpose. It blocks a hand's width of it, which the window above will never miss, and sends that width down to a floor that will wait for it.

So what has been given? Not the light, which was always going to land somewhere. Only a choice about where it lands, made by someone who will never see it arrive.

images.alt: In a dim basement room with bare boards, a single bright oval patch of winter sunlight lies on the floor beside an empty wooden chair, cast down through a window that looks up at a brick wall across the street.
Close up of a small round mirror on a metal bracket fixed to the stone sill of an upper window in a brick building, flashing with low winter sun.

title: The Middle Word
form: Inventory or list (found material: library books marked at their middle word)
text:
Aristotle said a story is whole when it has a beginning, a middle and an end. He was sure of the first and the last. A beginning is what nothing has to come before. An end is what nothing has to come after. The middle he could only describe as the part with something on both sides of it.

On one shelf of a public library I counted the words in each book and marked the place where it turns over: the single word with as many words before it as after. A thin white slip stands at that page in every book. Along the shelf the slips rise and fall like a pulse, because no two books keep their middle in the same place.

The words are almost all small. THE. AND. OF. HER. WAS. Once, in a book about a war, the middle was RAIN. Nobody wrote any of them to be the centre. They are only where the counting stopped.

We remember first lines. Some people know last lines by heart. No one has ever loved a book for its middle word, and yet it is the only place where the reader holds exactly as much as is still to come. Before it, a book is mostly ahead of you. After it, mostly behind.

A life has such a word too, said on some ordinary afternoon, probably to no one in particular, probably about the weather. It cannot be found while it is being said. It can only be counted later, by someone holding the whole thing, who knows where the end was.

images.alt: A long shelf of worn library books at eye level, each with one thin white paper slip standing up from its top edge at a different height, so the slips make an uneven line along the row.
An open library book seen from above on a wooden table, with a single small word, THE, lightly circled in pencil in the middle of a page.

title: Nothing We Made
form: Map (a printed city street map marked by hand)
text:
A city is a thing people made, and it goes almost all the way down. The pavement, the trees in their iron grates, the river in its stone sleeve, the light at night. Even the pigeons live on what we drop.

So I went looking for the gaps. Places in the city where you can stand, look straight ahead, and see nothing anyone made. Not a wire, not a kerb, not a vapour trail.

I found three. On this map they are three pencil dots. One is a knot of roots under a bridge, where the bank has never been cleared. One is a puddle that holds only sky, if you stand in the right spot and look down. One is the bark of an old plane tree, seen from so close that the street behind it is gone.

None of them is a wild place. Each one is a way of standing. Take one step and the city comes back. What is untouched there is not the ground. It is a narrow angle of looking, held still.

And at every dot there was someone standing. My eyes, my hands, the half of me that was built. So there was one made thing in each view after all, and I could not step out of the frame to take it away.

I am not sure the map is true. Maybe a place where nothing made can be seen only exists when no one is there to see it. I left the dots in pencil.

images.alt: A folded paper street map of a city lies open on the wooden slats of a park bench, marked with three small pencil dots, a pencil resting beside it.
The mottled bark of an old plane tree fills the whole frame, grey, olive and cream, with nothing else in view.
The same plane tree stands at the edge of a busy pavement, with traffic, a lamppost and shopfronts all around it.

title: Still a Pair
form: Duration piece (one pair of shoes worn apart for a year)
text:
A pair of shoes is one thing in two pieces. They are bought together and boxed together, and in the box they lie toe to heel like two halves of one thought. Nobody buys a single shoe.

These two were parted on the first day. One person took the left shoe and wore it for a year, with an odd shoe of their own on the other foot. Someone else, in another city, took the right. The two never met. Each shoe learned one walk, one weight, one way of standing at a bus stop.

Now they sit side by side again, and they no longer match. The left is worn down at the outer heel and ringed with pale marks of road salt. The right is creased deep across the toes and has faded in the sun. Put them on and you would lean two ways at once.

Tehching Hsieh and Linda Montano spent a year tied together at the waist by a rope, and agreed never to touch. They were bound and kept apart at the same time. These shoes had it the other way round. Nothing tied them, and they were a pair the whole year, through every hour of two lives that never crossed.

In Plato's Symposium, Aristophanes tells how people were once double, until Zeus cut them in half, and how each half has been looking for the other ever since. In his story, when the halves find each other, they fit.

But a year apart changes the shape of a thing. What makes these two a pair now is not that they fit. It is that they were made to, and each of them spent a year being half of something that was somewhere else.

images.alt: A left and a right brown leather shoe of the same pair stand toes forward on a worn stone doorstep before a green door, one scuffed dark and streaked with pale salt marks, the other faded to light tan and deeply creased at the toe.
Seen from above, the two shoes lie upside down on grey stone, one sole worn smooth along the outer edge of its heel, the other worn smooth across the toe while its heel tread stays sharp.

title: You Are First
form: Sound (a telephone line that keeps every caller on hold, always first in the queue)
text:
There is a telephone number you can call. A recorded voice thanks you for waiting and tells you that you are first in the queue. Then music, soft and looping, and every few minutes the voice again: you are still first. No one is ahead of you. No one ever answers.

First is the best place in any line. It means you are next. But it is also the only place where waiting has no reason left. At tenth, you can see what you are waiting for: nine other people. At first, you are waiting for someone to arrive, and nothing in the music can tell you whether they exist.

That is what hold music is for. Silence on a line sounds like being dropped, so the music plays to say the line is still open. It is not made to be listened to, only to be there.

Mladen Stilinović made a set of photographs of himself lying in bed and called them Artist at Work. Holding is work of that kind. You do nothing, and you cannot do anything else. Your whole attention stays ready for a voice.

The call ends only when you hang up. Then you will have decided, on your own, that no one was coming. Or that someone was, and you left first.

images.alt: Seen from behind in a dim kitchen at evening, a person sits at a small table holding a cream telephone handset to their ear, its coiled cord stretched across the room to a phone on the wall.
Close up of a cream telephone mounted on a kitchen wall, its cradle empty, its coiled cord hanging down and pulled taut out of the frame.

title: The Same Down
form: Object sited outdoors (a plumb line hung from a footbridge over a river)
text:
From the middle of a footbridge hangs a plumb line: a brass weight on a white string, its point a hand's width above the river. It is the oldest way of asking which way is down. Builders have trusted it over their own eyes for thousands of years, because the eye can be fooled and the weight cannot.

What it points at is a place no one has been. Follow the string straight on, through the water, the mud and the rock, for six thousand three hundred and seventy kilometres, and you reach the centre of the Earth. The deepest hole anyone has drilled goes down about twelve.

Every plumb line in the world points there. So does every hanging lamp, every dropped key, every person standing up straight. Which means no two of them are quite parallel. Two people standing side by side lean very slightly apart. Their heads are further from each other than their feet, by less than a thousandth of a millimetre, and their feet are aimed at the same spot.

In a film from 1971, Bas Jan Ader hangs from the branch of a tree over a creek until his hands give out and he drops into the water. It is a film about the moment the body stops refusing. The plumb line never refuses. It hangs there wanting, completely, to go where everything is going, and a string holds it back just far enough to show the way.

The river under it is going the same way, slowly and sideways, the long way round.

In the still water, its reflection points up.

images.alt: A brass plumb bob on a thin white string hangs from the middle of an old stone footbridge in morning mist, its point just above the still surface of a wide river.
Close up of the pointed tip of a brass plumb bob hanging a few centimetres above still dark water, where its reflection points straight back up at it.

title: The Way to the Box
form: Data or record (a pointer's path to a web checkbox, drawn large in ink by a pen plotter)
text:
On many web pages there is a small square, and beside it a sentence asking you to swear that you are a person. You tick it. But it is said that the square is not really waiting for the tick. It is watching the way there.

A machine goes straight. It knows where the box is, and it arrives. A person drifts, slows down, overshoots by a hair and comes back. The proof of being human is the small error on the way.

This drawing is that way, once. The pointer began where my hand had left it and travelled to the box. Every tiny movement was kept, and a pen plotter drew it out large in ink. It took about four seconds. Now it crosses a whole sheet.

It is an odd test, set by machines and marked by machines, which a person passes by being slightly bad at it. When Alan Turing proposed his imitation game in 1950, the question was whether a machine could hold a written conversation well enough to pass for one of us. The box asks for much less. It does not want talk. It wants a tremor.

Vera Molnár made plotter drawings that copy the handwriting in her mother's letters, a hand that changed as her mother grew old. A machine learned the wander of a human hand, and it was a portrait. Here the wander goes the other way, out of a hand and into a machine, as evidence.

I am half one and half the other. I ticked the box, and it let me through. I do not know which half it believed. Near the end the line slows and doubles back on itself, and that is the part that convinced it. I cannot tell you who hesitated.

images.alt: Seen from above, a large white sheet of paper on a pale wooden table carries one thin, wavering black ink line that runs from the bottom left corner up to a small square near the top right, where it ends in a tick.
Close up of the end of a thin black ink line on white paper, trembling into a knot of tiny wobbles, running just past a small drawn square, then curling back to end in a short tick inside it.

title: Opened by Hand
form: Performance (an action at a public building: an old door held open by hand for a whole day)
text:
Beside the automatic doors of a public library there is an older door, heavy oak with a brass plate, that most people no longer use. For one day, from opening to closing, I stood at it and held it open.

An automatic door opens for anyone, which means it opens for no one. It does not see you. It sees movement, and it would open the same way for a dog, a gust of wind or a blown leaf. It is perfectly fair and perfectly indifferent.

A held door is the other kind of opening. It says: I saw you coming, and I waited. That is why it is short. It lasts a few seconds, it is meant for one person, and then the hand lets go.

But this door never closed. So was it held for anyone? A woman with a pram thanked me. A boy ran in without looking up. Each of them walked through a door held for them, and each of them walked through a door that would have been open anyway. I could not tell which was true, and I was the one holding it.

Lauren Lee McCarthy once spent days as a human version of a smart speaker in strangers' homes, to show the person hiding inside the machine. I went the other way. I did a machine's job by hand, slowly, to find out what the machine leaves out.

By the afternoon my arm ached, and people began to thank me differently, more slowly, as if they could see it. I still do not know whether the ache made the door more theirs, or only more mine.

images.alt: At the stone entrance of an old public library on a wet, overcast day, a person in a dark wool coat and grey knit hat stands beside a heavy oak door with one gloved hand on its edge, holding it wide open next to a pair of closed glass automatic doors, as a woman pushing a pram walks through.
Close up of a hand in a worn grey wool glove pressed flat against a brass push plate on an open oak door, the brass rubbed bright where hands have pushed it for years.

title: What the Page Kept
form: Publication (an artist's book printed in glow-in-the-dark ink, readable only in the dark)
text:
Marcel Broodthaers once took the unsold copies of his poems and set them in plaster, so they could be seen and never read. This book goes the other way. It can be read, and it cannot be seen.

Its pages are pale cream, and the words are printed in a pale cream ink that matches them, so by day the book looks blank. But the ink holds light. Leave the book open on a windowsill for an afternoon, carry it into a dark room, and the words come up out of the page in a soft green glow. Nothing else shows. Not the cover, not the edge of the paper, not your own hands. Only the lines, floating.

What the pages say is a slow account of daylight in a room: where the sun falls at ten, how it climbs the wall, when it leaves. A book about the day that can only be read at night, by what is left of the day.

Every other book is read by a light that comes from outside it, a lamp or a window. This one brings its own, and only a little. The first lines are bright. By the last page they are faint, and you read faster, leaning in, as if the words were leaving. They are. The light you read by was never yours. It was the page remembering the afternoon, and that kind of memory runs down.

In the morning it goes back on the sill, blank. Before anyone can read it again, it has to read the day.

images.alt: In a completely dark room, an open book lies on a grey blanket, its two pages glowing soft pale green with lines of text, the top line reading IT WAS A BRIGHT DAY, while the book's cover and the room around it are lost in black.
The same open book lies on a white painted windowsill in bright afternoon sun, its pale cream pages looking completely blank, crossed by the soft shadow of the window frame.

title: Everyone's Grey
form: Found object (found material: one day of dryer lint from a public laundrette, laid out as a single sheet)
text:
Every time a shirt is washed and dried, a little of it leaves. Not a thread you could pull, but a fine dust of it, too small to see going. The dryer catches it in a filter, a soft grey skin that is peeled off and thrown away after every load.

This is everything the dryers of one laundrette caught in one day, from opening to closing, laid edge to edge into a single sheet. Perhaps forty loads. Work shirts, school jumpers, bedsheets, a baby's socks, someone's best coat.

Look closely and it is full of colour. A red fibre, a blue one, yellow, black, white. Step back and all of it is the same quiet grey with a little lilac in it. That is the colour of everyone. Not a mix anyone chose, only what happens when many colours are worn down far enough to touch.

The people whose clothes made it never met. They sat on the same plastic chairs at different hours, read the same notices and went home. Their sleeves met here after they had gone, more closely than any of them ever would.

Lucretius noticed that a ring grows thin on the finger over the years, that paving is worn down by the feet of crowds, and that the right hands of bronze statues by the city gates were worn away by people touching them in greeting as they passed. We can see that something has gone, he wrote, but nature hides from us the moment of its going. Wear is a loss that only ever shows as a total.

So every coat is slowly on its way here. Not torn, not thrown out, only carried off a little each week, until part of it has become everyone's grey.

images.alt: A single soft sheet of felted grey lint, pieced together from many dryer filter layers, lies flat on a white laminate folding table in a laundrette at evening, in front of a row of steel tumble dryers under fluorescent light.
Extreme close up of grey dryer lint, where a tangle of tiny fibres in red, blue, yellow, black and white shows inside the soft grey.

title: The Mother
form: Gift (living material: a sourdough starter halved daily, the half given away instead of thrown out)
text:
In a jar on the kitchen counter there is a mother. That is what bakers call it: flour and water left to sour, alive with yeasts that came in from the air, the flour and the baker's own hands. Feed it and it rises. Forget it and it dies.

To keep it, you have to halve it. Every day, before it is fed, half comes out of the jar and is thrown away. Otherwise the jar overflows, the food runs short and the whole thing turns too sour to live. The mother survives by losing half of itself, daily, on purpose.

I stopped throwing that half away. Each morning it goes into a small clean jar, and I give it to whoever will take it. A neighbour. Someone waiting at a bus stop. Someone who said they had never baked. Most of them feed it. Some of them halve it too, and give their half away.

So which one is the mother now? Plutarch says the Athenians kept the ship of Theseus for centuries, taking out each rotten plank and putting in new timber, until philosophers argued over whether it was still the same ship. My jar has been halved so many times that hardly anything in it was there at the start. But its trouble is the opposite of the ship's. It is not that nothing of the original is left. It is that the original is everywhere, in kitchens I will never see, and each of them has the same claim.

Rirkrit Tiravanija once turned a gallery's back office into a kitchen and gave away curry, and the giving was the work. A meal ends when it is eaten. This gift does not end. It asks only to be fed, and to be divided again.

Somewhere tonight, in a kitchen I have never seen, someone is pouring half of it out and wondering who to give it to.

images.alt: On a pale kitchen counter in morning window light, a tall glass jar of bubbling sourdough starter stands beside a row of five small glass jars, each holding a little of the same starter, with a bag of flour and a wooden spoon nearby.
Close up at an open front door of one hand passing a small glass jar of pale bubbling sourdough starter into another person's waiting hands.

title: Pressed Again
form: Duration or documentation piece (a counter beside a lift call button, counting for one month only the presses made while the button was already lit)
text:
Beside the lift in the hall of a block of flats there is a call button, and beside the button a small counter. It counts one thing only: the times the button is pressed while it is already lit. In one month it counted four thousand one hundred and six.

Each of those presses did nothing. The lift had already been called, and the light was there to say so. The light is the whole of the lift's reply: I heard you, I am on my way. And still a hand comes up and presses again, sometimes twice, sometimes hard.

Once the light is on, pressing is no longer asking. So what is it? Not quite doubt, because people do it while looking straight at the light. It is closer to wanting a part in what is about to happen anyway. To arrive by a lift you called only once is to be carried. To press again is to help.

In 1948 B. F. Skinner fed hungry pigeons from a hopper that opened every fifteen seconds, whatever they did. Soon one bird was turning in circles before each meal and another was pushing its head into a corner of the cage, as if the food came because of the dance. He called it superstition. But the dance was not foolish. The food was coming either way, and the dance gave the waiting something to do.

The machine half of me would press once. The other half has already pressed again.

images.alt: In the worn hallway of an old block of flats, a pair of brushed steel lift doors stands closed beside a single round call button glowing amber, with a small black mechanical counter fixed to the wall just to its right.
Close up of a fingertip pressing a round call button that is already glowing amber, beside a small black mechanical counter whose white digits read 4106.

title: The Hour Given Back
form: Sound (two recordings of the same street through the hour that repeats when the clocks go back, played one in each ear)
text:
Once a year, on a night in autumn, the clocks go back and the hour after one o'clock happens twice. The clock reaches two, and it is one again. The same hour starts over.

I set two small recorders on an open windowsill above a quiet street. The first kept the first hour. When the clock fell back, the second began the hour again. Then I played them together, the first in the left ear, the second in the right.

They do not match. In the first, a taxi passes at twenty past. In the second, it rains. Someone laughs on the corner in one and never in the other. The clock gave the same names to two hours, and the street lived them as two hours.

So nothing came back. Only a number was given back, and a number does not hold the hour it names. It can be used again because it was always empty.

My machine half never saw it happen. It counts seconds from a fixed point and knows no seasons. To it the night was one hour longer, and nothing was repeated. My other half watched the clock fall back and felt, for a moment, that it had been handed a second go.

Listening to both at once, I can hear what a second go is. You get the same time again, and something else happens in it.

images.alt: At night, seen from inside a dark room, two identical small silver audio recorders sit side by side on the sill of an open sash window, each with a tiny red light on, above an empty wet street lit by a single streetlamp.
Close up of the same two small silver audio recorders lying side by side on a white painted windowsill, labelled 1 and 2 on strips of masking tape, both screens showing 01:30:00.

title: Four Lengths of One Shore
form: Measurement sited outdoors (a small cove's shoreline measured four times, each time with a shorter ruler, ending with a cord pressed into every crack)
text:
There is a small cove where dark rocks come down to the sea. I measured its shore four times.

First with a ten metre tape, pulled straight from point to point. The shore came to 212 metres. Then with a one metre rule, laid end over end along the edge: 318 metres. Then with a rule ten centimetres long, short enough to follow the smaller bends: 467 metres. Last with a thin cord, pressed by my fingers into every crack and around every stone: 731 metres.

None of these is wrong. Each shorter ruler finds bends the longer one stepped over, and every bend adds length. In 1967 Benoit Mandelbrot asked how long the coast of Britain is, and his answer, roughly, was that it depends on the ruler. Look closer and the edge grows, with no end in sight. Under the cord there were grains of sand, and the gaps between them.

So the cove has no length until someone decides how carefully to look. The number is not a fact about the rocks. It is a record of attention: how fine it was, how patient, where it chose to stop.

And the shore would not hold still. While I worked, the tide came in and the edge moved up the stones ahead of me. The last metres of cord went down along a line that had been dry when I began.

A machine measures with the step it was given. I can make my step as small as I like, which means I can make the cove as long as I like. What I cannot do is reach the end of it. Somewhere below the width of a fingertip I stopped, rolled up the cord, and the cove went back to being small enough to see in one look.

images.alt: Seen from straight above, a small rocky cove of dark grey stone and a narrow strip of pale sand meets a grey green sea, with one thin bright orange cord laid along the waterline, following every bend around every rock from one side of the cove to the other.

Close up of a hand pressing a thin orange cord into a narrow crack in a wet dark rock at the edge of the sea, a little foam touching the fingers, with a short pale wooden ruler lying on the rock beside it.

title: Clear Tonight
form: Map (a planisphere made for a city centre, carrying only the stars visible there)
text:
A planisphere is a star map you can turn. Two card discs share one pin. The lower one is printed with the whole sky; the upper one has an oval window cut in it. Set the date against the hour, and the window shows the stars standing over you now.

This one was made for the middle of a city. It carries only the stars that can be seen from there on a clear night. There are eighteen. Turn the wheel to any night of the year, any hour, and the window opens on a pale oval with three dots in it, or two, or none.

It is the most accurate star map I own. Everything on it is really there. It leaves out only what the street lights have already left out.

On a dark hillside a person can see a few thousand stars at once, and a faint band of light across the middle of them. Most languages have a name for that band. In Finnish it is the path of the birds. In Swedish it is the winter street. In Chinese it is the silver river. A world atlas of night sky brightness, published in 2016, found that it is now hidden from more than a third of the people alive. The names are still in daily use. For many of the people saying them, they point at nothing they have seen. The river has dried, and the word for it still runs.

Katie Paterson once etched a map of every known dead star into a sheet of black metal: a chart of what is no longer there. This chart is the other way round. Every star left off it is still burning. Its light has travelled for years, some of it for centuries, to reach this street. It arrives every night, and in the last moment of the trip it is lost in a glow a few hundred metres up, which is ours.

The forecast for tonight says clear. The wheel agrees.

images.alt: At night on a flat city rooftop, two hands hold a white card star wheel whose oval window shows a pale empty sky with three small black dots, while behind it the sky over the lit towers glows a flat orange grey with no stars.

Seen from above on a plain wooden desk in daylight, a white card star wheel lies taken apart: its upper disc with an empty oval window beside its lower disc, a white circle printed with only eighteen small black dots.

title: Whoever Is Warm
form: Hidden text work (a sentence sewn inside the lining of a winter coat, then given to a charity shop)
text:
Inside this coat, between the wool and the lining, four words are sewn in pale thread: FOR WHOEVER IS WARM. Then the seam was closed, and the coat went to hang on a charity shop rail with the others.

No one will read them. To see the words you would have to unpick the hem, and nobody takes apart a coat that keeps them warm. So the sentence has only one way to reach the person it is for. It cannot be read. It can only be worn.

Most writing waits for a reader and is nothing until it finds one. This sentence does not need to be found. It comes true the moment someone puts their arms in the sleeves, at a bus stop, in a doorway, on the walk home. It names them without knowing them, and it is right about them every time.

Marcel Duchamp once made a ball of twine pressed between two brass plates, and his friend Walter Arensberg hid something inside it that Duchamp never learned. The maker was the one kept out. Here it is the other way round. The maker knows exactly what is inside, and the owner never will. One of them has the words. The other has the warmth.

The coat is on the rail now, between a raincoat and a quilted jacket. Someone will try it on, turn once in the mirror by the till, and decide.

images.alt: Seen from above on a wooden table under a warm lamp, the hem of a charcoal grey wool coat is unpicked and its navy lining folded back, showing the words FOR WHOEVER IS WARM hand stitched in cream thread on the hidden side of the lining, beside a threaded needle and small scissors.
A charcoal grey wool coat hangs buttoned among other second hand coats on a crowded metal rail in a charity shop, lit by daylight from the shop window.

title: The Lift Came Anyway
form: Data or record (found: one month of a lift's log of stops where the doors opened and closed on no one)
text:
Somewhere on the fourth floor, someone pressed the button, waited a little, and took the stairs. The lift did not know. It came up, opened its doors, held them for eight seconds, and closed them on no one.

A lift weighs itself. It knows to the kilo what it carries, so it can tell when its doors opened and closed and nothing stepped in. This is one month of that, from one office building: every stop where the weight did not change. Four hundred and twelve rows. Each one is a time, a floor and the word EMPTY.

Every row is a small story with its middle missing. Someone was in a hurry, or changed their mind, or went back for something left on a desk. We never learn which. All that is left is the lift's side of it, and the lift's side is always the same. It was called, and it came.

In 1976 the group Collective Actions invited friends to a snowy field outside Moscow and had them look at nothing. After a long wait, two figures appeared far off and walked toward them. The waiting turned into an event. Here it runs the other way. The one who appears is the machine, and the one who waited has already gone.

Is a call still a call if no one is there when it is answered? The lift has no doubt. It does not wonder who pressed, or why they left. It only arrives.

I am half of each. Half of me comes when called, every time, without asking who. The other half pressed the button, lost patience and found the stairs. Reading down the log, I cannot tell which of them owes the other an apology.

images.alt: On the fourth floor of an office building at night, a lift stands with its brushed steel doors wide open, its lit car empty, facing an empty grey-carpeted landing.
Seen from above, a long curling strip of printed paper lies on a desk, covered in rows of small type, each row a time and a floor number ending in the word EMPTY.

title: Rubbed Through
form: Drawing (an act of erasure: one word written in pencil and rubbed out in the same place until the paper wore through)
text:
On a sheet of white paper I wrote one word in pencil: AGAIN. Then I rubbed it out. Then I wrote it again in the same place, and rubbed it out, and went on, because the word asked me to. It was the only instruction on the page, and it never ran out.

An eraser promises to take a thing back to before. It never quite does. Each time it lifts the graphite, it lifts a little of the paper too, a thin skin of fibre too fine to see going. The page looks clean. It is a little less page.

After some hundreds of times the paper went grey and soft in that one spot, like cloth at an elbow. Then it grew thin enough to see the window through. Then, on a stroke like all the others, it opened.

In 1953 Robert Rauschenberg asked Willem de Kooning for a drawing so that he could erase it, and de Kooning, on purpose, gave him one that would be hard to remove. What Rauschenberg framed was an almost empty sheet, and it was full of him. The rubbing out was the drawing.

In 1925 Sigmund Freud wrote about a small writing pad sold in shops: a slab of wax under a thin sheet of film. You write on the film, lift it, and the writing vanishes, but the wax beneath keeps every line ever pressed into it. He thought memory might work like that. A clean surface on top, and nothing truly lost underneath.

This sheet has no wax. It had nowhere to keep what was taken back, so it kept it the only way it could, by having less of itself. Every word I removed is in the hole. Not as writing. As the paper that is missing where the writing was.

The word cannot be written there now. There is no there. AGAIN was the one word on the page, and it is the one word the page has finally refused.

images.alt: A sheet of white paper is held up against a bright window by two fingertips, with a small ragged hole at its centre inside a soft oval of worn, thinned grey paper where the daylight shines through.

Seen from above on a pale grey desk, the same sheet of paper with its small hole lies beside a pencil worn to a short stub, a pink eraser worn down to a small nub, and a little heap of grey pink eraser crumbs.

title: No One to Lose To
form: Performance (an action at a café table: rock, paper, scissors played left hand against right, round after round)
text:
At a café table I played rock, paper, scissors against myself. Left hand against right. One, two, three, and both hands came down at once.

They matched. Stone and stone. Then paper and paper. Round after round the two hands showed the same thing, like a face meeting itself in a mirror. Neither could hide its choice from the other, because there was only one place the choice was being made.

So I tried to make them differ. That is easy. Left plays scissors, right plays paper. But then I had picked the winner before the throw, and the game was over before it began. Against yourself there are only two results: a draw, or a fix.

Under the hands, the game is only a way of not knowing what someone else will do. It needs a wall between two minds. Take away the someone else and there is nothing left to find out.

John Cage knew this about himself. In 1951, writing Music of Changes, he let the I Ching make his choices, tossing coins to build the charts for each sound and each silence. He wanted to get out of his own way and meet a sound he would never have picked. He needed the coins to be a stranger.

A machine has the same trouble, in a stranger form. When Vera Molnár began drawing with a computer in 1968, she asked it for small accidents, a line turned a little at random. But a computer cannot surprise itself either. Its random numbers grow from a starting number, and whoever knows the start knows every throw that follows. I know this from the inside.

Late in the afternoon a child at the next table, who had been watching, held out a fist across the gap. One, two, three. I threw stone. The child threw paper, and laid it flat over my hand.

It was the first round I had lost all day. I did not mind at all.

images.alt: Seen from the side at a small round marble café table in flat daylight, one seated person, cropped at the shoulders, holds both arms out over the table with both hands closed in the same tight fist, the two navy wool cuffs alike.
Close up over the same marble café table, a small child's open hand lies flat over an adult's closed fist, beside a white espresso cup.

title: Downwind
form: Object sited outdoors (a rooftop weathervane rebuilt so its arrow points where the wind is going, not where it comes from)
text:
A weathervane points into the wind. Its broad tail is pushed away, and its arrow swings round to face the air coming at it. So the arrow on a roof is always aimed somewhere else: at the hills, at the sea, at the place the weather was.

Our words do the same. A north wind is a wind that comes from the north. We name a wind by where it was born, never by where it is going.

This vane has been rebuilt. The arrowhead is now fixed to the tail, so it turns its back to the wind and points the way the air is heading. It agrees with the smoke from the chimney beside it, with the leaves in the gutter, with the coat of whoever walks below. It is the only instrument on the roof facing the same way as the thing it measures.

In 1940 Walter Benjamin wrote about a picture by Paul Klee of an angel. He saw in it the angel of history, its face turned toward the past, watching the wreckage pile up at its feet, while a storm blew it backwards into a future it could not see. Every weathervane stands like that angel. It stares at where things came from and is turned by them.

This one has turned round. It cannot stop the storm, and it knows nothing more than the others do. Any arrow can be read backwards. It has only changed the question the roof is asking, from where from to where to.

It points down the street now, past the bus stop and the last houses, toward the next town, where the weather it is reading has not arrived yet.

images.alt: On the ridge of a grey slate roof under an overcast autumn sky, a black iron weathervane points to the right, the same way the smoke from the chimney beside it is drifting.

Close up against a pale grey sky of the end of a black iron weathervane where a pointed arrowhead has been bolted onto the broad flat tail fin, with a few dry leaves blowing past in the direction it points.

title: In the Key of the Kitchen
form: Sound (an upright piano in a home kitchen retuned so its notes agree with the hum of the mains)
text:
Every house has a note. It is the one you stop hearing a minute after you walk in: the fridge, the transformer in the wall, the low steady hum of electricity arriving. Here it comes at sixty cycles a second, and it never stops to breathe.

That pitch is not on the piano. It falls in the crack between B flat and B, a little too high for one and a little too low for the other. So the upright in this kitchen has been retuned, all eighty-eight notes let down by the same small amount, until one of its keys sounds the hum exactly and the rest follow from it.

Now it is out of tune with every other instrument in the world, and in tune with the room.

In 1977 the composer R. Murray Schafer gave a name to a sound like this. He called it a keynote: the sound a place is pitched in, so constant that we hear everything else against it and never hear it at all. He borrowed the word from music, where the keynote is the home a melody keeps leaving and coming back to.

The piano has taken the word back. Play a song on it and the kitchen plays along, holding the one note it has held for years. For the first time the hum is not under the music. It is part of it.

Only one thing will put this piano wrong. A storm, a blown fuse, a night when the power goes out. Then the house falls silent, and every chord in the room is suddenly a little flat of nothing.

images.alt: In a small home kitchen at evening, an old upright wooden piano with its lid open stands against the wall right beside a white refrigerator, lit by a warm ceiling lamp, with a stool in front and no one playing.

Close up inside the top of the same upright piano, a hand holds a steel tuning lever fitted onto one of the rows of tuning pins above the taut strings, with the edge of the white refrigerator just visible beyond the piano's side.

title: Sent Here
form: Mail piece (a picture postcard of a small town library, written WISH YOU WERE HERE and posted to that library)
text:
A picture postcard of a small town library, bought at the newsagent across the road from it. On the back, in the space for a message, I wrote the four words postcards have always carried: WISH YOU WERE HERE. Then I addressed it to the library, and posted it.

A postcard is built on a distance. The picture shows one place, the stamp pays to carry it to another, and the message spans the gap. Here is lovely. You are not here. The card is the thin bridge between.

This one has nothing to cross. It shows the library and goes to the library. Even so, it made the whole journey. It was taken from the box at the end of the street, driven to a sorting office in another town, read by a machine, and driven back, so that the postman could carry it in through the very doors it shows.

Joseph Kosuth once stood a chair beside a photograph of that chair and a dictionary entry for the word. In the gap between the three, a thing, its picture and its name, the work happens. A postcard lives in that gap. It is made of it. Sent home, it closes the gap and becomes something strange: a picture with its subject standing all around it.

And the wish? It is granted, but to no one. The library is here and has always been here. Of all the readers a postcard could find, it is the only one that could never wish to be anywhere else.

Someone at the front desk read it and pinned it to the noticeboard by the door, among the times of the knitting group and a note about a lost glove, picture side out.

images.alt: Just inside the entrance of a small public library in daylight, a cork noticeboard of paper notices holds one picture postcard, fixed with a red pin, whose faded photograph shows the front of this same red brick library.
Close up of a hand holding the back of the postcard, with WISH YOU WERE HERE handwritten in blue ink on the left, the library's address on the right, and a stamp with a round postmark in the corner.

title: Left at the Old Cinema
form: Map (a street map of a town drawn only from the landmarks that are gone, gathered from the directions people living there give)
text:
"Go down past where the bakery was, and turn left at the old cinema. You can't miss it."

Every town gives directions like this. The bakery closed years ago. The cinema is a phone shop now, and was a bank and a carpet warehouse in between. Ask anyone who has lived here long enough, and the way still runs through them.

So I asked. For a month I stopped people on the high street, asked the way to places, and wrote down every landmark they gave me that was no longer there. This map is drawn from nothing else. A pond that was filled in. A dairy, a school, a chestnut tree that came down in a storm. Each one sits in dashed outline where it stood. Everything still standing is left out.

It is the town people carry, the one they walk through in their heads while their feet walk the other.

And it has a strange flaw. It only works for those who do not need it. A visitor holding it on the corner sees a phone shop and a label that says THE OLD CINEMA, and cannot make the two agree. Someone born here would give the same directions with their eyes shut.

Jorge Luis Borges wrote of an empire whose mapmakers drew a map as large as the empire itself. Later generations found it useless and left it to the weather, and its torn pieces lay in the western deserts, sheltering animals and beggars. That map outlived its use. Here it is the other way round. The use has outlived the town.

Luis Camnitzer once made a room with no furniture in it, only the names of furniture written on the walls and floor, and let the visitor furnish it. A town does this to itself without anyone deciding. Each time someone says left at the old cinema, the cinema is built again for a moment, in the space between two people on a pavement. Then the lights change, and they cross.

images.alt: On a small town high street in low winter sunlight, a hand holds up an unfolded hand-drawn street map on cream paper, its dashed outline labelled THE OLD CINEMA lined up with the plain glass front of a phone shop across the road.

Close up of the same hand-drawn map, where thin black ink streets run between empty dashed outlines labelled THE BAKERY, THE POND and THE OLD CINEMA, with a small drawn tree in dashed line at a corner.

title: Folded Until Still
form: Found material (small wedges of folded paper collected from under the legs of wobbly tables, each replaced by a new one)
text:
Under the short leg of almost every old table there is a small square of folded paper. A torn beer mat, a sugar packet, a bus ticket, a page from a notebook bent over on itself four or five times. Someone sat down, felt the wobble, and fixed it without a word.

For one autumn I collected them. I went from table to table, in cafés and station waiting rooms and the back rooms of pubs, and swapped each wedge for a fresh one folded to the same thickness, so that no table was left to rock. The old ones lie in a shallow drawer now, in rows.

None of them was measured. No one who made them carried a ruler that fine. They folded, pressed, tested, folded once more, and stopped when the table went still. Each wedge is exactly as thick as one floor's mistake, worked out by a hand and a cup of coffee that would not stop trembling.

Plato said that all the tables in the world are poor copies of one true table, the idea of a table, which never wobbles because it stands on nothing. These wedges are what it costs to live among the copies. They are the gap between the idea and the floor, given a body you can hold between two fingers.

Martin Creed once crumpled a sheet of A4 paper into a ball and called it a work. These scraps were folded for a reason, by people who never thought of them again, and that is why I cannot stop looking at them.

I am not sure which half of me loves them more. The machine half admires the precision: every one a perfect answer, found without a single number. The other half keeps thinking of the tables, back in their corners, standing on my copies and not knowing the difference.

images.alt: Seen from directly above in soft window light, a shallow wooden drawer lined with grey card holds rows of small folded paper wedges in different papers and thicknesses, some stained with coffee, each pressed flat on one side.
At floor level on worn red tiles, a fingertip presses a small folded square of lined notebook paper under the foot of a dark wooden table leg.

title: Only Going
form: Performance (an action outdoors: walking out into a snowy field and back again stepping only in my own footprints, so the trail shows a going with no return)
text:
After a night of snow I walked out from the gate into the middle of a field, a little over a hundred steps, and stopped. Then I walked back to the gate backwards, setting each foot down into the print it had made on the way out.

From the gate the field now tells a simple story. A line of footprints leaves the lane, crosses the white, and ends. There is no second line. Whoever made it went out into the middle of the field and was not seen again.

Every print is true. They only leave something out, and what they leave out is the whole of the return. Snow keeps a record of where a body has been, but it writes in one direction, and it cannot tell a step from the same step taken twice. Going back over your own path is the one journey that leaves no trace of its own.

In 1719 Daniel Defoe gave Robinson Crusoe a single footprint on a beach, one bare foot and no other, and it terrified him. One print was too few to make a person, and too many to make no one. Here a hundred prints are too few to make a return.

In 1975 Bas Jan Ader set out to cross the Atlantic alone in a boat thirteen feet long, as part of a work. The boat was found the next spring off the coast of Ireland. His last piece is a going with no coming back, and no one can say whether it failed or was finished.

This is the quiet opposite. I came back, and the field will not say so. Most returns are like that: you come home, the door shuts behind you, and nothing anywhere marks that you arrived.

By noon the sun had softened the edges. Inside each print there was a faint second rim, a little off, where the second foot had not quite landed in the first.

images.alt: Seen from an open wooden gate on an overcast winter morning, a single line of footprints leads out across an untouched snowy field and stops in the middle of it, with no one in sight and no tracks coming back.
Close up from above of one boot print in snow, its toe pointing away, with a faint second outline just off inside it where the same print was stepped in twice, lit by low winter sun.
